title: Bakhchysarai
summary: Bakhchysarai is a city located in the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, [[ukraine|Ukraine]], known for its historical significance as the former capital of the Crimean Khanate and its cultural heritage. The city has a population of 27,448 according to the 2014 Census and has been under the occupation of the Russian Federation since 2014.

sections.heading: Geography
paragraphs: Bakhchysarai is situated in a narrow valley along the Çürük Suv river, approximately 30 kilometers southwest of Simferopol.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The earliest known human-made artifacts in the Bakhchysarai valley date back to the Mesolithic period, with settlements existing since Late Antiquity. Prior to the establishment of Bakhchysarai, the Qırq Yer fortress (modern Çufut Qale), Salaçıq, and Eski Yurt were constructed in the area, which later became part of the city.

Bakhchysarai first appears in historical records in 1502. In 1532, Sahib I Giray, who ruled as Khan of [[crimean-khanate|Crimea]] from 1532 to 1551, made it his residence, marking the city as the capital of the Crimean Khanate and a center for the political and cultural life of the [[crimean-tatar|Crimean Tatar]] community. The town faced significant events, including being sacked by [[cossacks|Cossacks]] in 1675 and burned during the Russo-Turkish War in 1736.

Following the annexation of the Crimean Khanate by the Russian Empire in 1783, Bakhchysarai lost its administrative importance but remained a cultural hub for the [[crimean-tatars|Crimean Tatars]], particularly under the influence of [[izmail|Ismail]] Gaspirali, who established the local newspaper Terciman in 1883.

During the [[crimean-war|Crimean War]] from 1853 to 1856, Bakhchysarai served as a hospital town for wounded Russian soldiers, although it was never captured by enemy forces despite its proximity to the front lines.

After the Russian Empire's collapse in 1917, Bakhchysarai became part of [[soviet-union|the Soviet Union]] in 1922. The city experienced the Sürgün, the deportation of Crimean Tatars on May 18, 1944, due to accusations of collaboration with Axis forces, resulting in a significant demographic change that lasted until their return in 1989.
Bakhchysarai became part of [[independent-ukraine|independent Ukraine]] in 1991 but was occupied by Russian forces during the [[russian-annexation-of-crimea|annexation of Crimea]] in 2014.

sections.heading: Name and Associations
paragraphs: The name Bakhchysarai has various spellings in different languages, including Crimean Tatar: Bağçasaray, Turkish: Bahçesaray, Russian: Бахчисарай (Bakhchisaray), and [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]]: Бахчисарай (Bakhchysarai). The name is derived from the Persian words باغچه سرای (bāghche-sarāy), meaning 'Garden Palace.'

In Russian literature, Bakhchysarai is romantically associated with Alexander Pushkin's poem 'The Fountain of Bakhchysarai' (1822), while Adam Mickiewicz wrote notable poems about the city in his 'Crimean Sonnets' (1825). Additionally, the asteroid 3242 Bakhchisaraj, discovered by Soviet astronomer Nikolai Stepanovich Chernykh in 1979, is named after the city.

sections.heading: Attractions
paragraphs: Bakhchysarai is home to several notable attractions, including Eski Yurt, Eski Dürbe, Chufut-Kale, Khan's Palace, Orta Cami Mosque, Tahtali-Jami Mosque, Cave Monastery, Zincirli Madrasa, and Tepe-Kermen. The city features a network of well-marked hiking trails connecting these sites.
From 2011, the town's Tourist Information Centre received support from the Czech Government and USAID, which was discontinued in 2014 following the Russian annexation of Crimea.

sections.heading: Demographics
paragraphs: In 1930, Bakhchysarai's population was recorded at 10,450, comprising 7,420 Crimean Tatars, 1,850 Russians, 315 Jews, 205 Greeks, 185 [[ukrainians|Ukrainians]], 50 Germans, 30 Armenians, 30 Bulgarians, and 365 others. By 2001, the population had grown to 26,700, with Russians forming the majority and significant minorities of ethnic Ukrainians and Crimean Tatars.

sections.heading: Education
paragraphs: The city hosts the College of Construction, Architecture and Design, a branch of the Crimean Federal University.

sections.heading: International Relations
paragraphs: Bakhchysarai is twinned with Bursa, Turkey, fostering international cultural and civic relationships.
